title: Influence of the manufacturing method on the adhesion of candida albicans and streptococcus mutans to oral splint resins

notes: Microbial adhesion to oral splints may lead to oral diseases such as candidiasis, periodontitis or caries. The present in vitro study aimed to assess the effect of novel computer-aided design/ com-puter-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) and conventional manufacturing on Candida albicans and Streptococcus mutans adhesion to oral splint resins. Standardized specimens of four 3D-printed, two milled, one thermoformed and one pressed splint resin were assessed for surface roughness by widefield confocal microscopy and for surface free energy by contact angle meas-urements. Specimens were incubated with C. albicans or S. mutans for two hours; a luminometric ATP-assay was performed for quantification of fungal and bacterial adhesion. One-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc testing, and Pearson correlation analysis were performed (p < 0.05) to relate manufacturing methods, surface roughness and surface free energy to microbial adhesion. 3D printing and milling were associated with increased adhesion of C. albicans compared to conven-tional thermoforming and pressing while S. mutans adhesion was not affected. Surface roughness and surface free energy showed no significant correlation with microbial adhesion. Increased fungal adhesion to oral splints manufactured by 3D printing or milling may be relevant for med-ically compromised patients with enhanced risk for developing candidiasis.
